clue.text: Nation pissed off authority

indicators.note: Milk that has gone off is no longer what it was, and letters in that state are not to be taken in the order handed over.

parts.note: twelve letters for the pile, taken for their spelling rather than their sense

explanation.surface: A whole country is furious with the people in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed off' reads as one phrase and the clue splits it: the first word joins the pile, the second is the instruction. British 'pissed' means drunk as well as angry, which is a second reason the eye slides past it.
explanation.definitionFit: Under the present dispensation means under the authority currently governing — the word naming the prevailing order and the licence it grants, not a person.

clue.text: Turned around holding working bomb part

indicators.note: Turning around leaves you facing the way you came, so the word in front is read from its far end.
Something holding another thing has it inside, so the two letters that follow go within what has already been assembled.

parts.note: a thing that has been turned has been rotated, seven letters before anything is done to them
a machine that is working is on, the state of the switch

explanation.surface: Somebody spins round with a live piece of a bomb in their hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working' is the crossword's standard two letters for a switch that is on. The word being turned is itself a synonym of 'turned', which is what makes the instruction so hard to separate from its fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The detonator is the small charge that sets the main explosive off, so it is literally one of the bomb's parts.

clue.text: Rainbow tattoo initially strange below small muscle

indicators.note: in a down clue, below puts the earlier pieces after the small muscle

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
pec is short for pectoral, a chest muscle

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of tattoo

parts.note: the word whose first letter is used
rum is an old-fashioned British word for strange or odd

explanation.surface: A rainbow tattoo, oddly placed beneath a small chest muscle.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum meaning odd, as in 'a rum business', is old British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectrum is the band of colours made when light is split, as seen in a rainbow.

clue.text: About to pass up duck

indicators.note: In a down entry up means read from the foot of the column, so the letters assembled in front are taken backwards.

parts.note: re is the 'about' at the head of a memo
to pass is the gentle way of saying to die

explanation.surface: A diner is on the point of turning down the duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass up' looks like one phrasal verb meaning decline, and the clue splits it: 'pass' is the euphemism for dying and 'up' is the instruction to read the column backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is the large northern sea duck whose breast feathers are collected to fill eiderdowns.

clue.text: Flower holding small, small volume you and I raised for person who follows

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the whole string is read upwards, from bottom to top
holding means the flower's letters wrap round the following letter

parts.note: a rose is a flower
a cc, a cubic centimetre, is a small volume
you and I together are us

explanation.surface: A gardener lifts a rose holding a small, small amount of water.
explanation.walkthrough: ROSE holding S gives ROSSE; add CC and US to get ROSSECCUS, and 'raised' turns the lot in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A successor is someone who comes after another, especially taking over a role or title.

clue.text: Toy with small amount of dessert

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a verb, to treat something carelessly or play with it
second meaning: a noun for a tiny quantity
third meaning: the British layered pudding of sponge, fruit, custard and cream

explanation.surface: Someone picks at a small helping of pudding without really eating it.
explanation.walkthrough: Three separate meanings of one word, with 'of' as the only joinery. In Britain a trifle is a cold layered pudding of sponge soaked in sherry, fruit, jelly, custard and whipped cream.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as a verb for dallying, a noun for something insignificant, and the name of a classic British layered pudding.

clue.text: Proposal from former queen

parts.note: in everyday British speech off does the work of from — you get something off someone
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the monogram of the queen who reigned until 2022

explanation.surface: A proposal arrives from a queen no longer on the throne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' looks like the joinery holding definition and wordplay together and is three letters of the answer instead. 'Former' is there because the monogram belongs to a queen who has died.
explanation.definitionFit: An offer is a proposal put to somebody, whether for a house or a job, and both are singular nouns.

clue.text: Iron covering meat served with blazing alcohol

indicators.note: Something covering another thing lies over it at both ends, so these letters close round the piece between them.

parts.note: Fe is iron's symbol on the periodic table, and it opens up to take the filling
four letters straight from the butcher's counter

explanation.surface: An iron lid covers meat that arrives at the table in flames.
explanation.walkthrough: Fe for iron is chemistry rather than the usual crossword abbreviation list, and it is one of the few symbols a setter expects you to carry. The definition is the whole of the second half — a way of cooking, not a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Food served flambé has brandy or rum poured over it and lit at the table, which is the definition word for word.

clue.text: Profess everything for example before end of June

indicators.note: What comes before a thing stands in front of it, so these pieces are placed ahead of the letter that follows.

parts.note: everything there is amounts to all
e.g. is exempli gratia, Latin for 'for example'

indicators.note: The end of a word is the letter it stops on, so only the final letter of the month is taken.

parts.note: the final letter of the month named

explanation.surface: Someone claims that everything has to be done by the end of June.
explanation.walkthrough: E.g. is one of the handful of abbreviations a setter drops in without further warning, and 'for example' is its full form rather than a hint about the definition. The month gives up a single letter and nothing else.
explanation.definitionFit: To allege something is to profess it as true while offering no proof, and both verbs take the same kind of object.

clue.text: Delayed imbibing last bit of hot drink

indicators.note: To imbibe is to take something in, so the letter that follows is swallowed inside the word before it.

parts.note: a train that is delayed is late, and the word opens up to take one more letter

indicators.note: The last bit of a word is the letter it ends on, and that single letter is all that is wanted.

parts.note: the final letter of the word 'hot'

explanation.surface: Someone running late swallows the last of a hot drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot drink' reads as one phrase and the clue splits it: 'hot' gives up its final letter, 'drink' is the definition on its own. 'Imbibing' belongs to the same café as the answer, which is how it passes as surface.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Drink' is the general class and this is one particular member of it — espresso topped up with steamed milk.

clue.text: Deft clue I arranged to be misleading

indicators.note: Arranged flowers are where the arranger wanted them rather than where they were, and letters arranged come out in a new order.

parts.note: nine letters for the pile, the setter counting himself in with the I

explanation.surface: A neatly built clue, put together by its setter to mislead.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes itself: a deft clue arranged to mislead is precisely what you are looking at. The I is the setter rather than the Roman numeral it usually stands for, and it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Deceitful and misleading are both adjectives for the same intent — leading someone to believe what is not so.

clue.text: Big first day back (almost)

parts.note: Mon, short for Monday, is the first day of the working week

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: the stern is the back of a ship

explanation.surface: Someone is relieved to be back almost after the big first day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' is not a reversal here; it is the stern of a ship, cut short by 'almost'.
explanation.definitionFit: Monster as an adjective means huge, as in a monster sale or monster truck.

clue.text: Make bigger part of integral network in retrospect

indicators.note: Part of something is a piece taken from inside it, so the letters wanted sit unbroken within the words that follow.
Looking back in retrospect is looking the other way, so the run is picked up from its far end.

parts.note: seven consecutive letters starting inside the first word and running across the gap into the second

explanation.surface: Looking back, the thing was part of an essential network.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts four letters into the first word and stops two into the second, which is why the eye slides straight over it. 'In retrospect' is the only signal that it then has to be read the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlarge a photograph or a house is to make it bigger, and the definition states that action plainly.

clue.text: Sushi meant to be chewed up with zeal

indicators.note: Food chewed up has been broken apart and no longer holds its shape, and letters in that state come out in some other order.

parts.note: ten letters for the pile, taken for their spelling rather than the meal

explanation.surface: Sushi that was intended to be eaten with relish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meant to be' reads as one phrase and only its first word joins the pile. 'Chewed up' does two jobs at once: the instruction, and exactly what the surface says is happening to the sushi.
explanation.definitionFit: Enthusiasm and zeal are both the eager energy somebody brings to a thing, and both are mass nouns.

clue.text: Unflappable setter's repeatedly embracing graduate

indicators.note: embracing means hugging, so the two contractions go around the word for graduate

parts.note: setter's read twice: as 'setter is' it gives I'M, and as 'setter has' it gives I'VE, the setter speaking
to pass is to get through an exam or course, to graduate

explanation.surface: The setter keeps hugging a graduate without getting flustered.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords the setter is 'I' or 'me'; the 's here is expanded twice, once as 'is' and once as 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Impassive means showing no emotion, calm and unmoved, so not easily flapped.

clue.text: Missing odd pieces of neoprene weapon

indicators.note: Missing the odd ones leaves the even ones, so the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the word are what survive.

parts.note: the even-numbered letters of the wetsuit material, read in the order they come

explanation.surface: Bits have gone missing from something made of wetsuit rubber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing' reads as a complaint about the neoprene and is the instruction. Épée is the heaviest of the three fencing swords, and the accents fall away when the word is written in English.
explanation.definitionFit: An épée is the stiff duelling sword used in fencing, so 'weapon' is simply the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Press release popular board finds fit to publish

parts.note: a press release is a PR in newsroom shorthand
what is popular is in, the way a colour is in this year
board is the table you eat off, as in board and lodging

explanation.surface: A popular board decides a press release can go out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' is the table rather than the committee the surface offers, a sense kept alive in 'bed and board'. 'Finds' is joinery, the verb that lets the sentence stand up.
explanation.definitionFit: Something printable is clean enough or sound enough to go into print, which is what fit to publish means.

clue.text: Irritating engineer in agony pierced by tip of needle

indicators.note: pierced by means something is stuck through it, so the needle's tip goes inside the jumble
to engineer something is to construct or contrive it, so the letters of in and agony are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the tip of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the word whose first letter is used

explanation.surface: A mechanic in pain after being jabbed by the point of a needle finds it irksome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engineer' looks like a person, but here it is a verb, signalling a rearrangement of IN AGONY.
explanation.definitionFit: Annoying means causing irritation or mild anger, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Announced reasonable ticket price

indicators.note: Something announced is said out loud, so the word beside it is wanted for its sound and not for its spelling.

parts.note: reasonable means fair, and said aloud that word can be written the other way

explanation.surface: The price of a ticket was called reasonable.
explanation.walkthrough: Fair and fare are pronounced identically and share no sense at all, which is the whole of the clue. 'Announced' is the signal that the sound of 'reasonable' is wanted rather than its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A fare is what you pay to ride — the sum printed on a bus or train ticket.

clue.text: In favour of period to rummage

parts.note: to be in favour of a thing is to be for it
an age is a period of time, the ice one or the golden one

explanation.surface: Somebody votes for a spell of rummaging.
explanation.walkthrough: The only real difficulty is that 'in favour of' is three words standing in for three letters. To forage is to hunt about for food, which is what animals and soldiers living off the land do.
explanation.definitionFit: To forage is to rummage about for something to eat, and both verbs take the same shape in a sentence.

clue.text: Programme rejigged at first to attract one learning the ropes

parts.note: the programme on a phone is an app

indicators.note: At first means at the very beginning, so only the opening letter of the word before it is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of the word 'rejigged' itself
to attract somebody is to entice them

explanation.surface: A programme is reworked from the start to draw in a trainee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejigged' is the trap: it reads as an anagram instruction and hands over only its own first letter. The programme wanted is the phone kind, three letters long.
explanation.definitionFit: An apprentice is someone learning a trade on the job, which is what learning the ropes describes — the phrase comes from sail.

clue.text: Earl fixes edits

parts.note: E is the peerage abbreviation for earl
to fix a broken thing is to mend it, and the third person keeps its s

explanation.surface: An earl repairs something.
explanation.walkthrough: A capitalised 'Earl' at the head of a clue reads as somebody's name and is a peerage abbreviation instead. All three verbs stay in the third person, which is what keeps the swap honest.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to edit it — the scholar's word for correcting what a manuscript got wrong.

clue.text: Pungent paste used to be on top of all baked Indonesian starters

indicators.note: In a down entry the piece on top is the one higher in the column, so these letters take the first cells.

parts.note: what a thing used to be, it was

indicators.note: A starter is whatever comes first, so the opening letter of each of the three words is taken.

parts.note: the opening letters of the three words, in the order they come

explanation.surface: A fiery paste that once went on top of a baked Indonesian starter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starters' belongs to the restaurant surface and to the wordplay at once, picking a letter from each of three words. Wasabi is the green Japanese horseradish served in a dab beside sushi.
explanation.definitionFit: Wasabi is that green paste, and its heat goes up the nose rather than across the tongue, so 'pungent' is the right kind of hot.

clue.text: In revolutionary prison uniform a lag originally wears for ceremonies

indicators.note: In puts the following pieces inside the reversed prison
wears, like a garment worn round the body, says the prison word goes around the other pieces
revolutionary means turning round, so the word for prison is read backwards

parts.note: stir is slang for prison
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: originally takes the first letter of lag

parts.note: the word whose first letter is used

explanation.surface: In a prison in revolt, an old convict dons the uniform for formal occasions.
explanation.walkthrough: A lag is British slang for a convict, but only its first letter is used. 'revolutionary' turns STIR round into RITS.
explanation.definitionFit: Rituals are set ceremonies performed in a fixed order, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Goatee that catches parts of comb

indicators.note: To catch something is to hold it fast, so the words in front are keeping the letters wanted between them.

parts.note: five consecutive letters running straight across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A goatee beard snags on the comb.
explanation.walkthrough: The hiding place straddles a word break, where the eye is least likely to look. Beard and comb belong to the same bathroom, so nothing in the surface sticks out as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The teeth of a comb are the thin prongs that do the combing, the mouth's word borrowed for a tool.

clue.text: Time left during task for a laugh

indicators.note: During a thing is in the middle of it, so these two letters are dropped inside the word that follows.

parts.note: a chore is a task, and it opens after its fourth letter
t is the standard single letter for time
l is the standard single letter for left

explanation.surface: There is time left over in the middle of a job.
explanation.walkthrough: Both single letters are standard, and the difficulty is seeing that 'time left' is two of them rather than one phrase about a deadline. Lewis Carroll coined the answer in Jabberwocky.
explanation.definitionFit: A chortle is a gleeful snorting laugh, a noun answering the noun the definition offers.

clue.text: Transport work freight

parts.note: a car is the everyday means of transport
a machine that works is said to go

explanation.surface: An order to shift a load of goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work' for GO is the sense in 'the engine won't go'. All three words can be read as nouns, which is what stops the definition standing out from the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Cargo is the freight a ship, lorry or plane carries — the load itself rather than the carrying of it.

clue.text: Explosive containing iodine beginning to rattle soldier

indicators.note: containing means the explosive word holds the chemical letter inside it

parts.note: a grenade is a small explosive device
I is the chemical symbol for iodine

indicators.note: beginning to picks the first letter of the word rattle

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: A bomb laced with iodine starts to rattle a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes inside GRENADE, near its end, and R from rattle is added last.
explanation.definitionFit: A grenadier is an infantryman, originally one who threw grenades, and now a Guards regiment soldier.

clue.text: Lodge one married posh girl from the East

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
m is how a form abbreviates married

indicators.note: In an across entry something coming from the east travels right to left, so those letters are written backwards.

parts.note: a deb is a debutante, the upper-class girl presented at court

explanation.surface: Putting up a married society girl newly arrived from the east.
explanation.walkthrough: Deb is short for debutante, the upper-class girl once presented at court to open the London season, so 'posh' is doing real work. 'Lodge' is the verb: a bullet lodges in a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbed a thing is to lodge it firmly in place, the i-spelling being the older variant of the same verb.

clue.text: Clearing house moving and removing right piece of furniture

indicators.note: moving the letters around means they are rearranged into a new order
removing tells us to take a letter out of the phrase before rearranging

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to work on

explanation.surface: A clearing house is relocating and getting rid of a fine piece of furniture in the process.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removing right' takes the R out of CLEARING HOUSE, leaving CLEAINGHOUSE; 'moving' then rearranges those twelve letters. A chaise longue is a long upholstered seat with a backrest at one end.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaise longue is a sofa-like seat for reclining, so it is an item of household furnishing.
